cards.title: Constant-factor approximation of graph crossing number
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Do there exist a universal constant \(C\geq1\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite undirected graph \(G\), outputs a drawing \(D\) in the plane satisfying \[\operatorname{cr}(D)\leq C\,\operatorname{cr}(G)\] with probability at least \(2/3\)?

cards.why: Crossing minimization is a basic graph-layout optimization problem with applications to drawing networks and circuit layouts. A constant approximation would establish a general algorithmic guarantee across sparse and dense inputs, beyond the degree-dependent and additive-error bounds currently available.
cards.status_note: Checked the original full question and drawing model, the 2022 full approximation theorem, the distinct 2023 hardness variant, and the 2025/2026 dense-graph theorem. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no universal constant-factor approximation or impossibility covering all constants. The randomized convention is explicit; the historical P ≠ NP hardness is stated only for deterministic algorithms.

progress.text: A fixed-factor inapproximability result establishes an obstruction to arbitrarily accurate polynomial-time approximation.
A subpolynomial approximation factor is obtained for bounded-degree graphs.
An additive-error approximation and drawing theorem yields asymptotically optimal approximation for dense graphs.

sentences: Draw every graph in the plane using at most a fixed constant times its minimum possible number of crossings.
The constant must be independent of the graph size and maximum degree.
The algorithm must construct a drawing in polynomial time; bounded-error randomization is allowed.
Existing low-degree and dense-graph results do not provide this guarantee for all graphs.
Hardness for one fixed ratio above one leaves open the possibility of a larger universal constant.

cards.definitions:
The input explicitly lists the vertices and edges of an unweighted graph. Parallel edges are permitted and counted separately, as in the source. Self-loops can be omitted because they can be drawn locally without crossings. There is no bound on degree, genus or crossing number, and no planar subgraph or embedding is provided. Running time is polynomial in the full input length on every random tape.

A drawing places vertices at distinct points and represents each edge by a simple polygonal curve joining its endpoints, without passing through any other vertex. The objective \(\operatorname{cr}(D)\) is the total number of pairwise edge crossings, summed over the entire drawing. The crossing number \(\operatorname{cr}(G)\) is its minimum over all drawings. One may restrict to good drawings: adjacent edges do not cross, two edges cross at most once, and no three edges cross at one point.

The output must specify a drawing, rather than only an unsupported estimate of its value. A finite combinatorial representation suffices: list crossings in order along each original edge and give a planar embedding of the graph obtained by replacing crossings with degree-four vertices. At each such vertex, the two segments of each original edge must be opposite in the cyclic order. This records the original curves and their crossings without requiring real-number coordinates.

Randomization with bounded error is explicitly allowed, in keeping with the later approximation literature; a deterministic algorithm would also qualify. The success probability is over internal coins for each fixed graph. The constant \(C\) and the polynomial time bound are independent of the graph. In particular, a factor depending on its maximum degree does not meet the target. When \(\operatorname{cr}(G)=0\), the approximation guarantee requires a drawing with no crossings.

This is ordinary topological crossing number. Edges need not be straight, there is no prescribed rotation system, and the objective is not the maximum number of crossings on any one edge. The source’s Multiple Edge Insertion problem additionally keeps a specified subgraph planar; that constraint is absent here.
cards.answer_criterion: Give such an algorithm and prove its running time and universal constant-factor guarantee, or prove that none exists. A conditional impossibility result must state its complexity assumption and cover randomized algorithms in the stated model. Hardness for a particular small approximation factor alone does not exclude all constant factors.

context_blocks.title: The existing hardness leaves room for a larger constant
context_blocks.text: Cabello proves that there is a constant \(c_{0}>1\) for which deterministic polynomial-time \(c_{0}\)-approximation is impossible unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), even on cubic graphs. This does not rule out an algorithm with some larger fixed factor. A randomized algorithm is not excluded merely by assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

context_blocks.title: Subpolynomial progress for low degree
context_blocks.text: Chuzhoy and Tan give a randomized approximation factor \(2^{O((\log n)^{7/8}\log\log n)}\operatorname{poly}(\Delta)\) for simple graphs with \(n\) vertices and maximum degree \(\Delta\). For bounded degree this is subpolynomial in \(n\), but still does not supply a universal constant.

context_blocks.title: Dense graphs admit much sharper approximation
context_blocks.text: Solé-Pi’s Theorem 1.2 constructs drawings with \(\operatorname{cr}(G)+O(n^{4}/(\log\log n)^{\delta})\) crossings, for an absolute \(\delta>0\), in randomized polynomial time. This yields asymptotic factor \(1+o(1)\) for dense simple graphs, but the additive error does not yield a constant multiplicative guarantee on arbitrary graphs with small crossing number.

context_blocks.title: A later hardness conjecture concerns a different objective
context_blocks.text: The 2023 paper studies maximizing the number of retained edges subject to a crossing budget. Its conditional hardness for Maximum Bounded-Crossing Subgraph should not be read as hardness of every constant approximation for the minimum total crossings of the entire input graph.

cards.context:
Cabello proves that there is a constant \(c_{0}>1\) for which deterministic polynomial-time \(c_{0}\)-approximation is impossible unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), even on cubic graphs. This does not rule out an algorithm with some larger fixed factor. A randomized algorithm is not excluded merely by assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

Chuzhoy and Tan give a randomized approximation factor \(2^{O((\log n)^{7/8}\log\log n)}\operatorname{poly}(\Delta)\) for simple graphs with \(n\) vertices and maximum degree \(\Delta\). For bounded degree this is subpolynomial in \(n\), but still does not supply a universal constant.

Solé-Pi’s Theorem 1.2 constructs drawings with \(\operatorname{cr}(G)+O(n^{4}/(\log\log n)^{\delta})\) crossings, for an absolute \(\delta>0\), in randomized polynomial time. This yields asymptotic factor \(1+o(1)\) for dense simple graphs, but the additive error does not yield a constant multiplicative guarantee on arbitrary graphs with small crossing number.

The 2023 paper studies maximizing the number of retained edges subject to a crossing budget. Its conditional hardness for Maximum Bounded-Crossing Subgraph should not be read as hardness of every constant approximation for the minimum total crossings of the entire input graph.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
